articles.title: Germany sets its sights on Russia's shadow fleet
articles.summary: The German government wants to follow other EU countries and take more decisive action against Russia's shadow fleet, accusing it of helping Moscow evade sanctions and carry out acts of sabotage.

image.caption: Royal Marine Commandos detain sanctioned tanker, the Smyrtos, in the English ChannelImage: LPhot Hutchins/Royal Navy/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions.

But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities, including acts of sabotage, espionage, and possibly drone operations and related disruptions."

Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party. In a recent interview with DW, she complained: "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table," she argued.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig

She accuses the German government of failing to take action: "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea, but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong."
Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet

By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel.

Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior."

In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety, or violate environmental regulations.
Russia's threats: Just a bluff?

It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint is aimed at avoiding an escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the small state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war."

Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded: "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened. Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely steered clear of confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels."

After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said: "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through."
Why did Norway seize a Russian ship for Ukraine?
Armed Russian crews on board

Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk: "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board. Those are risks that must be factored into the equation."

Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way.

"It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel."
Explained: How Germany will expand intel powers, and why
Inspections would raise costs for Russia

While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone. Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it."

He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy."
This article has been translated from German.
What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast.

articles.title: DENR puts WRMO in charge of water projects, NWRB to flag priority areas
articles.summary: MANILA – The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has assigned its Water Resources Management Office (WRMO) to oversee the water supply projects, while the National Water…

blocks.text: MANILA – The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has assigned its Water Resources Management Office (WRMO) to oversee the water supply projects, while the National Water Resources Board (NWRB) will identify priority areas for water supply development.

In a public advisory posted on Thursday, the DENR-Environmental Management Bureau (EMB) cited Department Administrative Order (DAO) No. 2026-35, which states that the WRMO is designated as the lead implementing and monitoring office for all DENR water supply-related projects.

The DENR said DAO 2026-35 aims to institutionalize the implementation of water supply projects, specifically the development of alternative water sources, water tanks, rainwater harvesting facilities, small water impounding systems, water filtration systems, water refilling stations, water service expansion, and spring development.

The WRMO shall be in charge of providing clear guidelines for the evaluation, implementation, monitoring and assessment of water supply projects to promote efficiency, accountability and transparency.
The WRMO is also tasked with defining the specific roles and responsibilities of the concerned DENR offices to ensure effective coordination and collaboration in project implementation.

It will review project plans and designs; coordinate with DENR offices, local government units (LGUs), local water districts (LWDs) and other stakeholders; monitor the progress and long-term sustainability of completed projects; and check compliance with environmental standards and regulations and facilitate partnerships for the development of water supply systems.
Priority areas
Section 5.1 of the DAO directs the WRMO to coordinate with the NWRB in determining where water supply projects are most needed.
The projects are intended to address water supply needs of LGUs, LWDs and communities, particularly those in small island, upland, and water-scarce areas.
The order defines water supply-related projects as programs and interventions meant to improve the availability, accessibility and quality of water for domestic and municipal use.

At the regional level, the Water Resources Utilization Section (WRUS) will gather baseline information on local water sources, existing service coverage and water demand to support the WRMO’s planning and prioritization.
The WRUS will also conduct site inspections and preliminary water quality and environmental checks; assist project beneficiaries in securing permits; and monitor ongoing and completed water systems.
Disaster assistance
The new rules also provide for DENR assistance to local water districts whose public water systems are damaged or disrupted by a national calamity or disaster.
Upon request of the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA) and recommendation by the WRMO, the DENR may provide technical and financial assistance to affected LWDs.

“Such assistance may include, but shall not be limited to, the assessment of water source integrity, rehabilitation of damaged pipelines or supply facilities, deployment of portable water treatment or purification units, and other appropriate interventions necessary to restore access to safe and potable water in affected areas,” Section 10 of the DAO read.

“The WRMO shall support the LWUA and other concerned agencies to ensure that emergency assistance is consistent with national disaster response protocols and aligned with available government resources,” it added, noting that all assistance shall be subject to existing budgetary, accounting, and auditing rules and regulations.
Project beneficiaries

The order covers LGUs, LWDs and other qualified entities as project beneficiaries, who will be responsible for providing project sites and logistical support, properly managing project funds, and operating and maintaining completed water supply systems.
They must also submit regular progress reports and allow DENR representatives to inspect and audit projects.
All water supply projects must comply with existing environmental, water resource and land-use regulations.
Depending on the project, beneficiaries may be required to secure environmental clearances, water permits and other permits from the appropriate agencies. (PNA)

articles.title: US crushes Hungary to reach Fiba Women's World Cup semifinals
articles.summary: BERLIN— Napheesa Collier scored 19 points and the U.S. routed Hungary 108-56 to advance to the semifinals of the women’s FIBA World Cup on Thursday. The U.S. will play the winner of the…

blocks.text: Hungary’s Ágnes Torok guards Napheesa Collier, of the United States, during the Women’s Basketball World Cup quarterfinal match between the United States and Hungary in Berlin, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi)
BERLIN— Napheesa Collier scored 19 points and the U.S. routed Hungary 108-56 to advance to the semifinals of the women’s FIBA World Cup on Thursday.
The U.S. will play the winner of the Spain-Australia game on Saturday in the medal round. France played China and Belgium played host Germany in the other quarterfinal matchups.

The Americans have now won 34 consecutive games in the tournament dating to a loss to Russia in the 2006 World Cup semifinals. The U.S. has made every medal round since 1983 when the format changed to have medal rounds.
It was a record-breaking performance for the U.S. The 108 points was the most by any team ever in a quarterfinal. The U.S. had 31 assists, again the most in this round.

“When that ball is moving, we want to get the best possible shot,” said Kahleah Copper, who had 10 points. “We want to make sure everybody gets involved. Everyone here on this roster, we know what they’re doing on their respective (WNBA) teams. But you come here, you sacrifice a little bit of that.”
Copper said the players were always looking to turn good scoring opportunities into great ones. The Americans did just that.

The U.S. was off and running early against Hungary, jumping out to a 36-12 lead after the first quarter. The Americans were constantly pounding the ball inside and converting turnovers into easy layups. Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese showed their growing chemistry on the court, finishing the quarter with a nifty pick and roll just before the buzzer. Collier had 10 points in the first 10 minutes.

The offense was sizzling early on as the Americans hit 20 of their first 26 shots (77%), including five of six 3-point attempts to race to a 50-18 lead with 6 minutes left in the first half. The Americans led 59-30 at the break — the highest scoring first half in team history in a knockout game at the event according to FIBA.
The Americans got a little scare when Sonia Citron had to leave in the third quarter when she was hit in the nose by a Hungary player’s hand by accident. Citron returned to start the fourth quarter.
Clark finished with 10 points and nine assists, just missing out on her second double-double of the tournament.

The U.S. was also solid on defense. They contained Hungary’s top scorer Dorka Juhasz, who plays for the Minnesota Lynx. She came into the game averaging 15.3 points and 11 rebounds in the tournament. She missed her first seven shots and didn’t get her first basket until 2:26 was left in the half. She finished the game with two points on 1 of 12 shooting.

Hungary came away with its best finish ever in the World Cup by reaching the quarterfinals for the first time. Hungary was fifth in the 1957 tournament but back then it was a round robin with no medal rounds.

articles.title: B.League: Gunma sweeps Manila games after OT win over Levanga
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The Gunma Crane Thunders ruled the Japan B.League Manila Games after defeating Levanga Hokkaido, 101-91, in overtime Thursday at Mall of Asia Arena. Gunma followed up its 98-81…

blocks.text: AJ Edu and Gunma Crane Thunders huddle during a game vs Levanga Hokkaido in the Japan B.League Manila preseason. –B.LEAGUE PHOTO
MANILA, Philippines—The Gunma Crane Thunders ruled the Japan B.League Manila Games after defeating Levanga Hokkaido, 101-91, in overtime Thursday at Mall of Asia Arena.
Gunma followed up its 98-81 win over Hokkaido on Wednesday night to sweep the Manila leg of its preseason.
The Crane Thunders trailed by five late in regulation, 85-80, before a 7-2 run tied the game at 87-all with 2:12 remaining in the fourth quarter.
Levanga’s John Harrar converted two free throws, but Takuto Nakamura answered with a bucket to tie the game at 89-all with 50.5 seconds left, sending it to overtime.
The extra period was all Gunma as the Crane Thunders raced to a 7-2 run for a 96-91 lead.
Yuma Fujii, who finished with 18 points, then knocked down a dagger 3-pointer to keep Levanga at bay, 99-91, with 42 seconds left.

Nakamura top scored for Gunma with 25 points while Stanley Johnson helped the cause with 17. Kerry Blackshear Jr. scored 12 while Filipino import AJ Edu flirted with a double-double after tallying nine points and nine rebounds.

Keisei Tominaga’s 34-point explosion went for naught in the loss. Dwight Ramos added 17 points, four assists, three rebounds and a steal, while Harrar posted a double-double with 15 points and 10 rebounds.

articles.summary:
Mike Rogers has also helped kill other bills that would have provided healthcare to responders and survivors

Mike Rogers, a Michigan Republican US Senate candidate, has sought in recent…

blocks.text: Mike Rogers, a Michigan Republican US Senate candidate, has sought in recent weeks to create controversy over old tweets his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed posted about 9/11. He has for example, falsely suggested El-Sayed, who is Muslim, said the US deserved the attack.

But, as critics have noted, Rogers has twice voted against healthcare and other benefits for 9/11 first responders and survivors, congressional records show. He has also helped kill other bills that would have provided benefits and healthcare to first responders nationwide. Rogers, a former member of Congress, is vying for Michigan’s open US Senate seat in a tight race that could decide control of Congress during the next session.

Rogers was among Republicans who voted against the 2010 James Zadroga Act to fund health care for 9/11 first responders and survivors, which was used in part to treat and monitor 40,000 people who worked in toxic conditions in the attack’s aftermath. The bills’ funding also helped treat responders for over 50 types of cancer linked to exposures at Ground Zero.

In committee, Rogers argued it “jeopardizes the financial health of the United States”. Rogers was joined by 156 other Republicans who voted against it, largely over its $5.1bn price tag, but 17 GOP members broke from the party and supported it. The final package passed the House over Rogers’ vote.

That drew sharp criticism this week from John Feal, a 9/11 first responder who has advocated and lobbied for legislation supporting benefit programs, and who spent 11 weeks in the hospital after a steel beam fell on his foot at ground zero. Part of his foot was amputated.

Feal told the Guardian he personally discussed the Zadroga legislation with Rogers on Congress’s floor during committee debate in which Feal testified. Feal said Rogers told him first responders’ health issues were a “New York problem” and asked: “Where is the money to help them going to come from?”
He called Rogers’ opposition to 9/11 first responder benefits “a betrayal”.

“Here’s the thing: Republicans like Mike Rogers love cops and firefighters until one gets shot or burned in a fire and can’t do his job,” Feal said. “That’s their playbook. They say: ‘You’re a hero. Oh, wait, you’re sick? You’re a drain on the municipality and the federal government. Get out of here.’”
The Rogers campaign did not respond to requests for comment.

The revelation comes after Rogers sent an email to supporters criticizing El-Sayed over his 9/11 comments, and appeared to lie about seeing Osama bin Laden’s body. In a bold typed section of the email, Rogers wrote: “I saw the dead body of Osama bin Laden with my own eyes, knowing that together, we had delivered justice for America.”

But Rogers was not in Pakistan when Bin Laden was killed by US special forces, nor was he in the White House Situation Room, where then president Barack Obama and senior administration officials followed the raid.

Republicans faced enormous backlash in 2010 for their votes against the Zagroda legislation. Feal at the time told CBS News: “Whatever member of Congress voted against this bill, whether Republican or Democrat, should go to jail for manslaughter.”
In 2002, Rogers voted against adding additional funding for veterans’ healthcare and first responders to a bill that compensated NYC schools for 9/11-related expenses.

In 2011, Rogers voted for a homeland security appropriations bill that was controversial over its deep cuts to funding for state and local first responders, as well as terrorism prevention funding. Several Republicans voted against it because of those issues. In 2013 and 2014, Rogers voted against amendments for budget legislation that included billions in funding for first responders. And in 2013 he voted against a proposal to protect pensions for first responders.

Henry Yanez, a retired Michigan firefighter, now a city council member in Sterling Heights, a suburb of Detroit, who has endorsed El-Sayed, was among those who went to New York City to support their fire departments in the 9/11 attack’s wake. He criticized Rogers for his votes.

“When you’re talking about the health and safety of our first responders, and now you’re going to kick the can down the road, you know – that’s a problem as far as I’m concerned,” Yanez said. “Mike Rogers – shame on him.”
Yanez said he is especially surprised because other Republicans in Michigan have supported first responders, and Rogers was an FBI agent. “He should get it,” Yanez said.
Feal said he believes Rogers’ opposition to the bills are disqualifying.
“Many members of Congress think they’re untouchable until they get humbled and get beat in an election,” Feal said. “Rogers is not invincible, and he’s just in this for himself.”

articles.title: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese having 'fun' playing together for USA
articles.summary: BERLIN— Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark’ s interactions are a subplot of the women’s FIBA World Cup, the WNBA season and if you spend enough time on social media, a divided country. Clark and Reese…

blocks.text: Angel Reese, of the United States, left, and United States’ Caitlin Clark warm up for the Women’s Basketball World Cup quarterfinal match between the United States and Hungary in Berlin, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi)

BERLIN— Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark’ s interactions are a subplot of the women’s FIBA World Cup, the WNBA season and if you spend enough time on social media, a divided country. Clark and Reese have shown their relationship on the court is thriving.

Both players are intense and animated competitors, and their fan bases’ are fiercely loyal. On much of social media you’re either for Reese or for Clark. It has that feel of rooting for Duke or Carolina; Yankees or Red Sox or Bird or Magic.

The pair have definitely bonded so far in the World Cup in their national team debuts. Clark said many of the stories about their relationship are “false takes,” saying she loves the fiery competitiveness that she and Reese share.

“No matter what, there’s always going to be people that create those narratives and say whatever they want to say,” Clark said. “There’s definitely no stopping that and they’re always going to be there. I think for ourselves, like I said, it’s easy for us to just come in here and compete.”
Reese has enjoyed playing with Clark as well as the other young members of the roster, including Paige Bueckers and Aliyah Boston.

blocks.caption: Czechia's Petra Holesinska guards Caitlin Clark, of the United States, during the Women's Basketball World Cup match between the United States and Czechia in Berlin, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026.

blocks.text: Czechia’s Petra Holesinska guards Caitlin Clark, of the United States, during the Women’s Basketball World Cup match between the United States and Czechia in Berlin, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi)

“We know each other’s game like the back of each other’s hand, she knows my spots,” Reese said of Clark. “We just continue to build chemistry because we know we’re going to be USA teammates for a while.”

In Thursday’s quarterfinal that the U.S. won 108-56, the growing chemistry showed. The pair had a nifty pick-and-roll to end the first quarter that ended with a layup by Reese. The Atlanta Dream forward returned the favor hitting Clark on a fastbreak for an easy lay-in later in the game.
“She’s got it for me a lot of times so it’s probably finally due for me to get one to her and she easily finished it,” Reese said smiling.

Clark and Reese have played together on the 2024 WNBA All-Star team that beat the U.S. Olympic team, but they will forever be joined at hips after their clash in the 2023 NCAA title game catapulted them into the center of debates.
Reese’s LSU squad topped Clark’s Iowa team in the matchup, but the players actions and interactions (who can forget Reese pointing to her ring finger in the closing seconds), drew attention to them.
Clark said she appreciates Reese’s desire to win and her relentlessness on the court, saying “it’s been fun to to be able to play with her.”

Clark laughed recalling one incident in the tournament between she and Reese that has gotten some attention. When Clark was subbing in during the opener against China and started to step on the court before being officially told to, Reese, who was entering the game at the same time, pulled her back off the court.
“Well, the ref had gotten mad at me a couple of times prior, so she was saving me from the ref getting mad at me again,” Clark said laughing.

In another fun moment, Reese was talking to the media after the tight win over Italy and Clark ducked past her, apologizing for interrupting her interviews. Reese smiled and gave Clark a high-five as she went by.

They’ll be back on opposite sides soon enough — Reese’s Atlanta Dream and Clark’s Indiana Fever are both headed for the WNBA playoffs and both have 26-14 records. They could meet in the first round if the current seeds hold.

But for now, they share a common goal and the fact that Reese and Clark say they are having fun on the court together is good news for U.S. women’s basketball fans. The duo could be part of a core group of players expected to be teammates in the next several Olympics.

articles.title: Sara Duterte camp files urgent motion for TRO vs. grave threats charges
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte has filed before the Supreme Court an urgent motion to resolve her application for a temporary restraining order in the grave threats case filed against her…

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 10:07pm

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte has filed before the Supreme Court an urgent motion to resolve her application for a temporary restraining order in the grave threats case filed against her before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court.
The motion was filed on Monday, September 7, after the filing of the charges on Friday, September 4, and Duterte posting bail on Saturday, September 5.
Her arraignment is scheduled for Friday, September 11.

"With the evident haste by which Petitioner's criminal prosecution continues to move, there is a real and present danger that the reliefs sought in Petitioner's Amended Petition - the restraint of criminal prosecution of an incumbent impeachable officer under the constitutional rule of limited procedural immunity, will be rendered moot and academic, if immediate injunctive relief is not now obtained," the motion read.

"The imminent arraignment and pre-trial demonstrate that the criminal proceedings are not merely threatened but are actively and rapidly progressing, notwithstanding the serious and far-reaching jurisdictional and constitutional issues to be resolved. This would render nugatory the reliefs sought, and irreversibly deprive Petitioner and her office of the constitutional protection she seeks to be enforced by this petition," it added.
The Department of Justice on August 11 filed grave threats charges against Duterte in connection with remarks she made in an online press conference in 2024.

In the presser, Duterte said she had already talked to someone to kill President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and then Speaker Martin Romualdez if anything happened to her.

The Vice President's camp on August 21 filed a motion for certiorari and prohibition against the informations filed before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, asking for an injunction on the cases and that they be rendered void.

"As shown, Respondents' acts of investigating and indicting Petitioner in violation of the Vice President's limited procedural immunity from suit during tenure and the clear provisions of the 1987 Constitution constitute urgent and compelling grounds for this Honorable Court to immediately restrain further action thereon by issuing Petitioner's sought TRO and/or Writ of Preliminary Mandatory Injunction. Immediate injunctive relief is imperative to prevent Respondents from further circumventing this constitutional immunity, interfering with the Vice President's performance of her office, and irreparably damaging our tripartite system of government," the motion read.

"This Honorable Court has consistently held that injunctive relief may issue upon showing that: (a) there exists a clear and unmistakable right to be protected; (b) this right is directly threatened by an act sought to be enjoined; (c) the invasion of the right is material and substantial; and (d) there is an urgent andparamount necessity for the writ to prevent serious and irreparable damage," it added.
The Duterte camp filed another motion on September 4, asking the SC to order the recall of the warrants.
A spokesman for Duterte said she would attend the arraignment "as required by law." —NB, GMA News

articles.title: English winemakers expect ‘vintage year’ after record-breaking summer heat
articles.summary:
Hot weather means sweeter grapes, but outlook gloomier for beermakers, as drought diminishes barley harvest

English sparkling winemakers expect their earliest grape harvest and a…

blocks.text: English sparkling winemakers expect their earliest grape harvest and a “vintage year” after a scorching summer quickly ripened grapes.
However, beer sellers have warned of a potential shortage after record-breaking temperatures and a drought hitting much of England has caused poor yields of barley.
Nyetimber, which was the first producer in England to grow pinot noir, chardonnay and pinot meunier exclusively for sparkling wine, has 11 vineyards in West Sussex, Kent and Hampshire.

It has announced it will begin picking grapes on 14 September for this year’s harvest, the earliest since the company planted its first vines in 1988. The winemaker’s next earliest harvest was in 2018, when the first grape was picked on 19 September.

Nyetimber said this harvest, for which it has recruited 500 pickers, will yield almost 2,500 tonnes of grapes, which could result in more than 1.5 million bottles of sparkling wine being produced from the 2026 vintage.

Because of the late spring frosts, it is expected the harvest will be slightly smaller than usual, but that the large number of sunny days this year will have concentrated the sugar in the grapes, meaning 2026 could be a vintage year. The company’s first vintage was Blanc de Blancs 1992, which won numerous wine prizes.

Nyetimber’s head winemaker, Cherie Spriggs, said: “This year brings another unprecedented vintage as we begin harvesting earlier than ever. We are excited to taste the fruits of our labour, which as always has come with certain challenges: late spring frosts that affected almost 30% and the summer drought, which has decreased the size of certain berries. However, the hot and sunny weather has helped to balance out these factors, giving us strong potential for fantastic wine quality.”

Though winemakers are celebrating, the outlook is gloomier for beer aficionados. Lisa Hogan, who runs the Diddly Squat Farm in Oxfordshire with her partner, the TV presenter Jeremy Clarkson, has said there may be “less beer all around” after extreme weather led to a poor barley harvest.

blocks.caption: Diddly Squat Farm in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire is run by Hogan and Clarkson. Photograph: Stephen Dorey/Alamy

blocks.text: This summer was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’s hottest since records began in 1884.

Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis, driven by burning fossil fuels. August was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world, with global temperatures reaching 1.65C above preindustrial levels, scientists said on Thursday, amid warnings of further heating on the way.
Hogan and Clarkson make Hawkstone Lager on their farm, which has been made famous by the Amazon show Clarkson’s Farm.

Hogan said: “I think a lot of barley farmers suffered … And funnily enough, last year our yields were terrible, but the quality was better. This year, after a second year of dry weather, both the harvest and its quality have suffered.” She said farmers were struggling to irrigate crops, leading to poor yields.
The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board has said the barley harvest could be the worst on record and said yields were running 19% below the five-year average last month.

Hogan added that other countries are facing similar difficulties: “It is a struggle because if you have another bad harvest, you won’t be able to supplement, say, by getting grain in from Poland. So, we just have to pay a higher cost, and then we have to try not to pass that on to the customer.”

articles.title: Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots
articles.summary:
While England makes its first foray into unfamiliar territory, it’s proved a boon for Italy’s cash-strapped municipalities

A nightly tourist tax may be

blocks.text: A nightly tourist tax may be unfamiliar territory in the UK, but countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades.
Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs.
Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats.

Similar measures were later implemented in France, Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors.
Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination.

The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy.
Depending on the destination, and sometimes the hotel type, the nightly fee typically ranges from between €1 (£0.86) and €10 per person, although guests of five-star hotels in Milan pay €12.
Venice has also had an entrance fee in place since 2024, although that is only targeted at day-trippers.

The overnight levy is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations. In 2024, Rome made €222.4m, followed by Milan (€109.3m), Florence (€82.9m) and Venice (€38.9m), according to data from Siope, the finance ministry’s tracker of public money flows.

The revenues are supposed to be spent on local services, especially in towns and cities buckling under the pressure of overtourism, or on maintaining monuments. However, the reality is that cash-strapped municipalities use it for other expenses.
after newsletter promotion
“All municipalities want the fee because they need the money,” said Gianluca De Gaetano, manager of the Rome unit for Federalberghi, the hotels’ association.

Tourists mostly just absorb the payment, even if begrudgingly. “They tend to complain when they find that the services in a city are not up to par, especially if they’ve already paid a lot for their accommodation,” said De Gaetano.

articles.title: Man and woman arrested in London on suspicion of aiding Iran’s foreign intelligence
articles.summary:
Arrests of woman, 42, and man, 60, made after Met carried out searches of addresses in north and north-west London

A man and a woman have been arrested by counter-terrorism police in London…

blocks.text: A man and a woman have been arrested by counter-terrorism police in London on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service.
The arrests of the 42-year-old woman and 60-year-old man were made after searches at addresses in north and north-west London on 24 June, the Metropolitan police said.
A third property was also searched in north-west London on 9 September after their arrest under the National Security Act (NSA).
The investigation is not linked to attacks at buildings and venues linked to Jewish and Iranian communities in London, the force added.
It is also not thought to be linked to any activity or events linked to the Jewish high holy days period.
The man and woman have been released on conditional bail until a date in October.

Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing London, said: “We know that news of these arrests will come as a concern to some members of the public, but I want to stress that we do not believe there to be any imminent threat to the wider public in connection with this matter.
“We’ve seen a marked increase in the tempo of our work linked to national security and state threats over the past year and this investigation is a continuation of that.
“As we’ve shown here, if we suspect any activity could threaten the safety of the UK or the public, then we will not hesitate to take action.

“I would also like to remind the public that the overall terrorism threat level is at severe, so we continue to ask for everyone’s support through being vigilant, and if you see or hear anything that doesn’t look right, then please, trust your instincts, and report it to us.”

articles.title: CESAFI SEASON 26: SCSC Baby Warriors escape DBTC in thriller
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — The San Carlos School of Cebu (SCSC) Baby Warriors held off the Don Bosco Technical College (DBTC) Greywolves, 65-64, in a thrilling Cebu Schools Athletic Foundation, Inc.…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — The San Carlos School of Cebu (SCSC) Baby Warriors held off the Don Bosco Technical College (DBTC) Greywolves, 65-64, in a thrilling Cebu Schools Athletic Foundation, Inc. (Cesafi) Season 26 high school basketball game Thursday, Sept. 10, at the Cebu Coliseum.
The victory put the Baby Warriors in the win column after a winless campaign last season, improving their record to 1-1. The Greywolves, meanwhile, dropped to 1-2.
DBTC came out firing and built an 11-point lead, 34-25, early in the second period before SCSC quickly turned the momentum around.
The Baby Warriors surged ahead, 37-35, at halftime and continued to dictate the pace in the second half, stretching their lead to 10 points, 54-44.
The Greywolves refused to go away, however, trimming the deficit to six heading into the final period and setting up a tight finish.

The teams were tied at 62 with 54.7 seconds remaining when John Philip Sardido sank crucial free throws to put SCSC back in front. The Baby Warriors then added to their lead on a fastbreak layup, while Heath Lauren Macapil also delivered four points down the stretch.
DBTC outscored SCSC, 18-11, in the final period but could not complete the comeback after Christian Lambayan missed a potential game-winning layup in the closing seconds.
Lance Luther Aballe and Macapil led the Baby Warriors with 13 points apiece, while Ahron Andrei Casul added 10.
Zane Ondoy paced the Greywolves with 14 points, followed by Antonio Joseph Issifu with 13 and Lambayan with 11.

articles.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations
articles.summary: As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers, while keeping her loyal older fans.

image.caption: In recent years, she's renewed her image by opting for more expressive fashionImage: Martin Harris/Captital Pictures/picture alliance

blocks.text: On September 12, Celine Dion kicks off a series of 26 sold-out concerts, part of a Paris residency held through May 2027. Some 500,000 people are expected to attend the performances, marking the global star's highly anticipated return to the stage following a prolonged break.
In 2022, she announced that she was battling with a rare and incurable neurological disorder, stiff-person syndrome. The health issues led her to cancel her world tour.
In the summer of 2024, she returned to the spotlight atop the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics, her resilience giving hope to fans worldwide.

Now, in the days ahead of her Paris concerts, Dion has been thrilling hundreds of fans gathered in front of her hotel, taking the time to chat with them for a few minutes every day, sometimes even joining them in spontaneous sing-alongs and dances.

blocks.caption: Charming her fans with candid moments at the Royal Monceau Hotel in ParisImage: Cyril Pecquenard/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The best-selling Canadian artist of all time, Dion has released a total of 27 studio albums, sold more than 200 million records worldwide and earned multiple Grammy Awards.
Even though her most defining hits date back to the 1990s, she is more than a nostalgia act, as her appeal is now skyrocketing with Gen Z and millennial listeners.
How did that happen?

blocks.caption: 'It's All Coming Back to Me Now': Her power ballads are surging in popularity againImage: Joel Goodman/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A modern fashion darling

In her daily exchanges with her fans on her way to rehearsals, she's always wearing fresh couture pieces: an asymmetrical Loewe gown, a bold blue Givenchy leather dress by Sarah Burton or a striking jacket by Tom Ford.
"Celine Dion is turning the streets of Paris into her runway," wrote Vogue magazine in reaction to her stylish outfits.

"She's always really been into fashion, already in the 1990s, even though we long didn't know this," says Quebec cultural reporter Stephane Leclair, author and host of a podcast series on the star's "D'eux" album. "You know, Celine Dion was never considered 'cool.' She's always had that slightly corny, slightly goofy side. But through her genuine interest for fashion, she’s managed to revamp her image quite a bit."

A notable move came in 2016: Dion admired Zendaya's edgy red carpet looks so much that she tracked down her stylist, Law Roach, and asked him to team up with her. She credits Roach with transforming her into a modern fashion darling.
But that's just one aspect that explains her ongoing — and renewed — popularity.
A rags to riches story

Born on March 30, 1968, Celine Dion was the youngest of 14 children of a poor family in French-speaking in Quebec, Canada. As she proudly notes on her official website, the house was so full that, as a baby, she had to sleep in a drawer instead of a crib.

She grew up surrounded by music, and recorded her first song at the age of 12. It impressed music manager René Angélil so much that he mortgaged his house to pay for her first record. She quickly emerged as a child star in Quebec.

blocks.caption: Her winning performance at the Eurovision Song Contest in 1988Image: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Inspired by Michael Jackson, she decided that she wanted to become a megastar. She won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 1988 and launched her first English-language album, "Unison," in 1990.
This, however, sparked cultural tension among French-speaking fans in Quebec, who felt she was neglecting her roots to pursue American and international superstardom.

"We were between two referendums on Quebec's independence at the time," points out Leclair. But even after she became a global star, she proudly kept identifying as the "little girl from Charlemagne," the small town near Montreal where she grew up.
"People in Quebec quickly understood that it didn't change anything, that she would always remain one of them, and that it only added another layer to her career," notes the cultural reporter.

Indeed, she also kept working in French all while building her career as a global pop artist. Teaming up with popular French song-writer Jean-Jacques Goldman, they released "D'eux" in 1995. It became the best-selling French-language album of all time.

The theme song for "Beauty and the Beast" (1991) won her both a Grammy and an Academy Award, while her best-selling "My Heart Will Go On" (1997) for the blockbuster film "Titanic" cemented her status alongside music's greatest vocalists.
Adding groundbreaking edge to Las Vegas

While other aging stars would head to the Las Vegas Strip to finish their careers, Dion revolutionized the music industry with "A New Day...," her high-profile residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace: With a total of 714 performances from 2003 to 2007, she demonstrated how such residencies could be modern, cutting-edge — and extremely lucrative.
It served as a blueprint for Las Vegas residencies by younger stars, such as Britney Spears and Adele.
Viral authenticity

"The world's biggest stars are often dead set on protecting a perfect, untouchable image. Celine, on the other hand, is incredibly accessible. She isn't afraid to let her true, authentic personality shine through," points out Leclair.
"And Celine's die-hard fans just love her humorous side," he adds. "They love the fact that she's a bit wacky. It makes her really relatable."

Famous for spontaneously breaking into song during interviews, those moments, as well as various over-the-top scenes from her 1990s music videos, have been picked up in Internet memes and TikTok trends.

Encouraged by her teenage sons, she launched her own official TikTok account in January 2026. She went viral with a "What's in My Bag?" video where she pulls out a mix of everyday essentials and completely unhinged items.
Writing a new chapter
But beyond the humor, she's also ready to share her most vulnerable moments.
In 2016, she lost her husband — her manager, René Angélil — and a brother to cancer within the same week. Her 2019 album "Courage" focused on loss and recovery.

blocks.caption: Their 26-year age gap and the fact that Dion was only 12 when she met her manager and future husband made headlines, but they stayed together until his deathImage: Ryan Remiorz/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Her 2024 documentary "I am: Celine Dion," in which she looks back on her life and career all while addressing how she deals with her stiff-person syndrome diagnosis, has been praised by critics as intensely sincere and visceral.

One scene of the film follows her as she suffers from a painful spasm: "I don't think many stars of that caliber would have agreed to be filmed — and have the footage included in the final cut — in such an unflattering state," notes Leclair. "It was partly out of a desire for transparency, to explain to her fans why she had to step back."
And her fans highly value this authenticity, as well as her resilience.

She is now undergoing physical and therapies to manage her symptoms and be able to perform again for this series of more than 2-hour-long concerts. They will feature 18 musicians and four backing singers; a live choir will also join them on stage for several songs.

articles.title: Uganda: Traditional kingdom plunged into succession crisis
articles.summary: A royal succession committee and the family of late King Oyo Nyimba of Toroo have put forward competing candidates. Questions have been raised as to whether the late monarch indeed had a son as his…

image.caption: Oyo Nyimba (center) at his official coronation in 2010Image: Samuel Egadu/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Uganda's traditional kingdom of Tooro has been plunged into a sucession crisis after the family of late monarch Oyo Nyimba rejected on Thursday other clan members' choice of successor.
Although Uganda is a republic, it contains several ancient kingdoms whose leaders are still held in high regard as keepers of tradition and maintain significant social influence.

Oyo, who was also known by his regnal name Rukidi IV, became the world's youngest monarch at the age of three in 1995 following the death of his father. His ascension celebrations were attended by longtime Ugandan strongman President Yoweri Museveni.
His reign was overseen by a series of relatives acting as regents until he turned 18 in 2010.
He died on August 27 at the age of 34 while undergoing cancer treatment in the United States.
Who are the main players in the succession fight?
On Wednesday, the royal clan's succession committee named the late king's cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the next monarch.
Kijanangoma is a television anchor at public broadcaster UBC.
However, Oyo's mother and sister announced on Thursday that they rejected this proposal, indicating that the king had left a will declaring his son his successor.
His mother Queen Kemigisa called the committee a "self-appointed group of clan members" who had named a new king despite knowing the contents of Oyo's will.
She also accused the Ugandan military of placing her family under house arrest.

The identity of Oyo's son and the son's mother remains a mystery. A campaigner for HIV/AIDS prevention and environmental causes, he had not publicly acknowledged a son until Toroo's Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki announced the boy's existence after Oyo's death.

The controversy grew after Andrew Mwenda, a well-known journalist and relative of Oyo's, wrote on social media site X that a son could only succeed a father in Toroo if he was born to a queen, and said that the family had not produced so much as a picture of the boy.

Prime Minister Armstrong called for both sides to remain calm on Thursday, saying the process "should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our King still awaits burial."
Oyo's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

articles.title: ECB raises interest rates to fight off inflation jump
articles.summary: The European Central Bank raised borrowing costs and warned that inflation could remain high for an extended period. Energy markets and geopolitical tensions are still major concerns.

image.caption: Amid mounting inflationary pressures and a shaky energy market, the ECB has decided to tighten its policyImage: Jana Rodenbusch/REUTERS

blocks.text: The European Central Bank (ECB) raised interest rates on Thursday, hoping to curb rising inflation driven by higher energy costs stemming from the war between the US and Iran. This is the second increase that the ECB has had to implement this year. Risingoil and natural gas prices pushed inflation above 3% in the 21-country eurozone, surpassing the previous target of 2%.
"The outlook remains highly uncertain, with risks to the upside of inflation and to the downside of economic growth," the ECB said in a statement after its annual meeting, held this year in Berlin.

The ECB also announced its economic growth projection for 2026. The study reveals slight growth of 0.9% compared to 0.8% in June, and inflation is now expected to average 3.0% this year and 2.5% in 2027.

Without a clear resolution to the US-Israel conflict with Iran, which began in late February, energy costs continue to rise, suggesting persistent inflation. There is also growing concern about gas storage levels, which remain below historical norms as the winter heating season approaches.
Why Iran fuel crisis hits different in Europe than the US
Economic outlook remains uncertain
"The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period," according to the ECB.

For countries in the eurozone, another hike in rates means more expensive mortgages, consumer credit, and loans. There has been little indication that eurozone inflation is being passed more broadly through the economy via higher prices for food, goods, or services.

Experts say the European Central Bank is worried about raising rates too slowly again. The last time it needed to take measures at this pace was in 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"The inflation outlook has worsened over the summer," said Sylvain Broyer, chief economist for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa at S&P. "Supply shocks are not only multiplying, but it is increasingly likely that demand is also contributing to inflation," he said.

articles.title: India-China thaw: 5 things to know as Xi heads to Delhi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to India for a summit on Saturday that could mark the biggest step in a cautious thaw after years of hostility between the two countries.…

blocks.text: NEW DELHI, India — Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to India for a summit on Saturday that could mark the biggest step in a cautious thaw after years of hostility between the two countries.
Xi’s visit for the September 12-13 BRICS summit would be his first trip to India since October 2019 and follows Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s August 2025 visit to China.
The nuclear-armed Asian giants have been slowly improving ties since a deadly 2020 border clash. Flights, some visas and high-level contacts have gradually resumed.
But deep mistrust remains, with their disputed Himalayan frontier, a heavy trade deficit and strategic rivalry complicating ties.
Here are five things to know:
Border comes first
The relationship was transformed by the June 2020 Himalayan border clash, when fighting in Ladakh killed 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers.
In October 2024, Beijing and Delhi agreed on patrolling arrangements, paving the way for renewed political contacts.
But the underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometer (2,175-mile) high-altitude border along Tibet.
“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
“You cannot have a buildup of your forces on the border… but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.'”
The Dalai Lama also lives in exile in India, ever since the Buddhist spiritual leader fled the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, after Chinese troops crushed an uprising in 1959.
Beijing condemns the Dalai Lama as a rebel and separatist.
Unequal trade ties
China is now India’s largest trading partner, with bilateral goods trade reaching $151 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to Indian government data.
But the relationship is heavily tilted toward Beijing.
India imported $131 billion of goods from China, while exports were $19 billion, leaving a record $112 billion trade deficit.
Modi’s government is pushing domestic manufacturing and seeking to reduce dependence on China for machinery, electronics, chemicals and industrial components.
But Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said India needs Chinese technology.
“India… need China’s — not just investment — but more and more technology,” he said.
China, he added, also wants to expand trade “even though India keeps complaining about the trade imbalance.”
Partners and rivals
Both are members of BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO).
Taneja argued that for Beijing, Xi’s “primary reason” for the visit is to bolster BRICS as an “alternative institution” to US-dominated institutions.
But they are also competitors.
India’s security partnership with Washington, including its participation in the so-called Quad security alliance with Japan and Australia, is viewed warily by Beijing.
China’s close relationship with India’s arch-rival Pakistan is viewed with concern by New Delhi.

“The very fact that President Xi is coming to India does indicate that… even if it’s because of the turbulence in the world caused by America, the two countries want a working relationship,” said Ashok Malik of The Asia Group.
Confidence-building measures
Ties have slowly warmed since 2024. That includes moves to revive border trade across their Himalayan frontier, ease visas and allow Indians to resume a key Hindu pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.
Direct flights, suspended for more than five years, resumed in October 2025.
“The relationship is now being put back on track,” said Harsh V. Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation.
“But it is more stabilization, rather than any dramatic change.”
Test, not breakthrough
Modi and Xi last held formal bilateral talks at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025.
Their brief interaction at this month’s SCO summit in Bishkek offered another public signal of a thaw.
But analysts remain cautious.

“The mistrust between India and China is so huge,” said Pant. “Unless there is a demonstrable shift in Chinese behavior, it is very unlikely that many in India would buy the India-China friends narrative.”

articles.title: China extends anti-dumping probe into pecans from US, Mexico
articles.summary: BEIJING, China — China has extended an anti-dumping investigation into pecans from the United States and Mexico, Beijing’s commerce ministry said on Thursday, two weeks before an expected visit…

blocks.text: BEIJING, China — China has extended an anti-dumping investigation into pecans from the United States and Mexico, Beijing’s commerce ministry said on Thursday, two weeks before an expected visit by President Xi Jinping to Washington.
The probe launched last year was originally expected to expire on September 25, one day after President Donald Trump’s anticipated meeting with Xi in the US capital.
The investigation has now been extended until March 25 next year, the Chinese commerce ministry said in a statement on Thursday, citing “the complexity of this case.”
Beijing began imposing steep levies of 54.3 percent on pecans from the United States and between 17.8 percent and 51.6 percent on those from Mexico in August.
The fees were initiated after the commerce ministry’s “preliminary ruling” found that pecans were being dumped in the Chinese market, “causing substantial damage to the relevant domestic industry.”
The United States and Mexico are the world’s biggest producers of pecans.
US exports of the nuts to China were worth $93.1 million in 2023, according to the US Foreign Agricultural Service.
The row over pecans adds to rumbling frictions in trade relations between the world’s top two economies, which escalated sharply last year following Trump’s return to the White House.

Beijing and Washington reached a shaky truce late last year in a tit-for-tat tariff war initiated by Trump, although China’s towering trade surplus and fierce technological competition still spur tensions.

articles.title: PCG continues search for 86 missing after Palawan ferry fire
articles.summary: MANILA – The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) is searching for 86 people still missing after a fire broke out aboard the passenger Ro-Ro cargo vessel MV June Aster off Coron, Palawan, on Wednesday.…

blocks.text: MANILA – The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) is searching for 86 people still missing after a fire broke out aboard the passenger Ro-Ro cargo vessel MV June Aster off Coron, Palawan, on Wednesday.

In a press conference at the PCG National Headquarters in Port Area, Manila Thursday, PCG spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said 43 survivors and five casualties have so far been confirmed, based on the manifest submitted by the vessel’s captain showing a total of 134 people on board, comprising 117 passengers and 17 crew.
The vessel, owned and operated by Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc., departed the Port of Batangas at around 8:13 p.m. on Tuesday and was set to arrive in Coron at 6 p.m. the following day.

Cayabyab said the PCG received a report of the fire at around 6:45 p.m. on Wednesday from an employee of the shipping company, prompting the immediate deployment of PCG assets, as well as nearby vessels, private floating assets and fisherfolk in the area.

She said the swift response was consistent with the agency’s “10:30 doctrine” under its Intensified Community Assistance, Awareness, Response and Enforcement (iCARE) program, which requires small assets to be deployed within 10 minutes of an incident report.
As of Thursday, the fire had not yet been declared out, with the PCG vessel BRP Suluan reporting thick smoke still emanating from the ship.
PCG personnel have not yet been able to board the vessel due to the continued presence of smoke, which poses a suffocation risk to responders.
“Our topmost priority, aside from conducting the search and rescue, is to ensure the safety of our responders,” she said.
The vessel appears to have drifted due to strong currents and wind, with its position shifting from about 4 nautical miles off Barangay Turda to around 7.6 nautical miles as of Thursday.

The PCG is coordinating with coastal barangays and has broadcast radio advisories asking vessels and aircraft in the area to watch for unusual floating objects and report possible sightings of survivors.
Search operations are also being guided by the PCG’s Search and Rescue Optimization Planning System, a science-based tool that factors in wind and current data to estimate possible drift locations.
On the cause of the fire, she said one survivor recounted hearing a loud explosion near the cargo hold before smoke and flames quickly spread through the vessel.
She declined to speculate on the cause, saying a comprehensive investigation is underway.
“We will not give a conclusive statement,” she said, adding that the testimonies of survivors and crew would form part of the investigation.
The PCG is also looking into whether the shipping company may be held liable, including whether the crew was negligent in its response once the fire broke out.
The agency is still verifying reports that two Chilean nationals may have been among those on board, along with the identities and roles of the survivors already rescued.
She noted that some of the 43 survivors did not have life jackets when rescued, saying the explosion and fire likely caused passengers to jump overboard immediately.

The ship passed a Vessel Safety Enforcement Inspection on March 10, 2026, and was found compliant with safety requirements, including having enough life jackets on board for its certified capacity of 333 passengers and crew.
Most of the 43 survivors were brought to Coron District Hospital, with some already discharged as of Thursday, she said.
She added that PCG commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan has directed the intensification of pre-departure inspections for all vessels nationwide following the incident. (PNA)

articles.title: Are electric vehicles really bad for the environment?
articles.summary: Some German politicians are calling for a delay to the EU plan to phase out gas-powered vehicles, saying cars must be judged on the entire carbon footprint. But the full picture still says EVs are…

image.caption: The electricity used to charge EVs can contribute to carbon emissions, if it comes from burning fossil fuels like coal and gasImage: Gero Rueter/DW

blocks.text: "The EU's car lie" — Germany's Bild tabloid newspaper didn't mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union's "dangerous" claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral.

Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media, he called for an end to "the EU's phaseout of internal combustion engines" set for 2035. Such a policy shift, he said, was now backed by "science."

Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU's climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered "climate-neutral."
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure

The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only "41% on average" over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix.

Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle's entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling.
It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM.
No new insights in TUM report

Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation think tank, said TUM's analysis didn't offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known.

Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80%.

Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car's brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don't match fully electric vehicles.

Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe.
Batteries have a high environmental cost

Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water.

The ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine.

blocks.caption: While lithium-iron phosphate batteries tend to be cheaper and last longer, nickel manganese cobalt batteries deliver more power and work better in colder climatesImage: Rodrigo Freitas/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production," Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they're generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture.

Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans.
Czechia's lithium mine plans spark resistance
Renewable energy making the case for EVs

The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don't produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas.
But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs.

blocks.caption: Home solar power installations have taken off in Germany, giving EV owners a cheaper way to charge their carsImage: Daniel Reinhardt/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Europe's electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonised and expected to be almost fully decarbonised by 2040," said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. "As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will also only strengthen the case even more."

Clark said it wasn't necessary to replace the EU's current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules.

"Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector," she told DW in an email. "Their replacement of ICE vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed."
Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth
Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy.

"The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think," he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia.

blocks.caption: EV sales have increased in Asia in recent years, with China's BYD leading the packImage: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns.
"We cannot win the race by ignoring it," said Bieker. "[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down."
Ethiopia's EV boom: A role model for all?

articles.title: Eight-gold target set as Philippines eyes Asian Games splash
articles.summary: Bannered by star athletes Carlos Yulo, Alex Eala, EJ Obiena, and Annie Ramirez, Team Philippines seeks to breach the four-gold mark in an Asian Games edition for the first time since 1962

blocks.text: EIGHT. Athletes, coaches, and officials during Team Philippines' send-off for the 2026 Asian Games and 2026 Asian Para Games.
Philippine Olympic Committee's Facebook page
Bannered by star athletes Carlos Yulo, Alex Eala, EJ Obiena, and Annie Ramirez, Team Philippines seeks to breach the four-gold mark in an Asian Games edition for the first time since 1962

items: Team Philippines aims to win at least eight gold medals at the upcoming Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, doubling their previous best of four golds.
To motivate the athletes, additional allowances and bonuses have been announced for exceeding past medal tallies, with the Asian Games set to begin on September 19.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Team Philippines has not won more than four gold medals in the Asian Games for over six decades, but the ambitious goal for the upcoming edition in Nagoya, Japan, is to win twice as many.

Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham “Bambol” Tolentino on Thursday, September 10, said the target for the quadrennial showpiece is at least eight gold medals, believing the 464-strong delegation can surpass the four-gold hauls each in 2018 in Indonesia and in 2023 in China.

“I’m not going to put any pressure on the athletes for this Asian Games. There will be no pressure, but give it everything you’ve got. Give it your absolute best,” said Tolentino in Filipino during the athletes’ send-off at the Rizal Memorial Coliseum.
The Philippines last breached the four-gold mark in the 1962 edition, where it clinched seven gold medals to finish fifth overall.
All but one of the Philippines’ four gold medalists in 2023 are still around, with Gilas Pilipinas, pole vault stalwart EJ Obiena, and jiu-jitsu standout Annie Ramirez aiming to defend their thrones.
Jiu-jitsu veteran Meggie Ochoa, another champion in 2023, has already retired from the national team and transitioned into coaching.
Aside from the three returning titleholders, gold medals are expected from gymnastics ace Carlos Yulo and tennis star Alex Eala.

Yulo, the Philippines’ first and only Olympic double gold medalist, bagged the floor exercise crown in the Asian Artistic Gymnastics Championships in June, while Eala has posted promising results, winning her first-ever WTA Tour title at the Washington Open in August, in between a fourth-round appearance in Wimbledon and a third-round stint in the US Open.
Other gold-medal prospects, according to Tolentino, come from boxing, taekwondo, wushu, mixed martial arts, athletics, esports, and skateboarding.
“There are no replays here. Give it everything you’ve got,” said Tolentino.
In a bid to motivate the delegates, Philippine Sports Commissioner chairman Patrick “Pato” Gregorio announced an additional P6,000 allowance for each participating athlete and coach.
Gregorio also promised bonuses if the country exceeds the four-gold Asian Games tally and 10-gold Asian Para Games yield in 2023.
“Let us achieve more, and when you come back, you will have a very good Christmas, I assure you,” said Gregorio. “Let us make the Filipino nation smile.”

The Asian Games will officially open on September 19 and run until October 4, but the men’s basketball tournament already started, with Gilas Pilipinas kicking off its title defense against Bahrain on Friday, September 11. – Rappler.com
