articles.title: DILG: 2M loose firearms circulating in PH
articles.summary: The Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Thursday said there are an estimated two million loose firearms in the country.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 7:19pm
The Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Thursday said there are an estimated two million loose firearms in the country.

During the budget hearing of the DILG at the Senate, Secretary Jonvic Remulla said they were using the agency’s confidential funds for intelligence gathering ahead of their proposal to amend the so-called Robin Padilla Law.

The Robin Padilla Law is the nickname of Republic Act (RA) 8294, which amended Presidential Decree No. 1866, the law setting the rules for firearms. RA 8294 made the unlawful possession of firearms a bailable offense.
“We estimate in the range of the high of two million,” Remulla said when asked by Sen. JV Ejercito how many unlicensed firearms there were nationwide.
Ejercito was surprised by the number, saying that it used to just be 500,000 to 600,000.

“Ninety-eight percent of the crimes committed in the Philippines use loose firearms so we feel it best that if we do catch them and we do have search warrants, that the charges be non-bailable,” Remulla said.
The owners of loose firearms tend to be recidivists, Remulla said. Once they post bail, they go out and commit another crime.
The remaining two percent of armed crimes were from licensed guns, and they were usually committed within homes or in some instances, when a child gets their hand on the firearm, the DILG chief said.

Remulla said the DILG is also moving for greater accountability in gun ownership. It said there should be equal accountability for the owners of licensed firearms should someone steal their gun and use it to commit a crime. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film
articles.summary:
Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian

Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders ​on…

blocks.text: Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders ​on the secret ​systems used in ​the war on Gaza​ has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.

NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at the Venice international film festival on Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award.

The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack. Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians.

Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities.

The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families.

blocks.caption: Israeli soldiers at a military position overlooking the so-called yellow line in Gaza in May. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP

blocks.text: The Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed.

The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.
Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”.

“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement.

The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.”

blocks.caption: An explosion after an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on Wednesday. Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/AP

blocks.text: The documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.

NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere.

Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”.

Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”.

“It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.”

Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population.

Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation.

Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.
Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.

Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank.

“In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”

articles.title: Remulla: Talks ongoing to arrest Bato dela Rosa, warns operation may turn deadly
articles.summary: The authorities are closer to catching Sen. Ronald "Bato" Dela Rosa, who is wanted on account of a warrant of arrest for charges of crimes against humanity from the International Criminal Court, even…

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 7:07pm

The authorities are closer to catching Sen. Ronald "Bato" Dela Rosa, who is wanted on account of a warrant of arrest for charges of crimes against humanity from the International Criminal Court, even as talks are ongoing to take him into custody, Interior Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla said.
Remulla said many lives may be lost if law enforcement goes on "full operation" to arrest the senator.
Asked about the chances of the police capturing Dela Rosa, Remulla said, "Yes, lumalaki na."
(Yes, it's getting more likely.)
Remulla indicated the importance of negotiations to bring in Dela Rosa.

“If we go on a full operation, maraming mamamatay (many people will be killed)... because of the nature of the operations. A lot of people will be put in jeopardy, so the negotiations are ongoing, we’re… and we will smoke him out sooner or later,” Remulla said.
Remulla made the remarks after the Department of the Interior and Local Government presented before the Senate Committee on Finance its proposed budget for 2027.
The Philippine National Police earlier said that 20 firearms that were linked to Dela Rosa have been surrendered.
Asked if this was an indication of negotiations, Remulla said he could not comment about it.
“Iwan inyo muna sa amin 'yun kasi it’ll jeopardize the operations,” Remulla said. (Leave it to us because it might jeopardize the mission.)

Dela Rosa has been issued an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in relation to the drug war, which killed at least 6,000 people during the term of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
Duterte is already detained at the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands, for crimes against humanity. —Jean Mangaluz and Ian Cruz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Apart from timing, what else is ‘unusual’ about Romualdez’s hospital confinement?
articles.summary: Romualdez’s admitting physician reveals that he did not see nor examine the former House speaker when he was confined on September 7 because the attending physicians barred him from entering the room

blocks.text: EX-HOUSE LEADER. Speaker Martin Romualdez graces the first meeting of the Visayas Caucus of the 20th Congress in the House of Representatives on August 7, 2025.
House of Representatives
Romualdez’s admitting physician reveals that he did not see nor examine the former House speaker when he was confined on September 7 because the attending physicians barred him from entering the room

items: Former House speaker Martin Romualdez was hospitalized on September 7 after an arrest warrant for plunder was issued against him, but his condition was deemed a non-emergency by his admitting physician.
Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan testified that Romualdez did not require hospital confinement, and the medical certificate did not specify a need for recuperation time.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Apparently, the condition of former House speaker Martin Romualdez was not an emergency case when he rushed himself to the hospital on September 7, the day Sandiganbayan 3rd Division issued an arrest warrant against him for plunder.
Dr. Kurt Allen Sibayan, Romualdez’s admitting physician, said this in court on Thursday, September 10, during the hearing on the former speaker’s motion for hospital confinement.

Rappler saw a copy of Romualdez’s medical certificate, which did not indicate the number of days the former speaker needed for recuperation. On the floor, Office of the Ombudsman Deputy Special Prosecutor Omar Sagadal reiterated this point twice: Romualdez doesn’t need confinement.
“There’s nothing here that says the patient requires confinement,” said Sagadal.

Romualdez is currently confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City after admitting himself at around 4 pm on Monday. He gave a list of diseases, including hypertension and heart problems.
He was served the arrest warrant by the Philippine National Police on Monday, but he has yet to be transferred to a jail facility because of his condition.

During the hearing, Sibayan also revealed that he prepared the abstract, but did not see nor examine Romualdez. The physician said he was told that resident doctors were not allowed to go inside the room.
It was attending physician Dr. Rosalio Torres (hematologist), Romualdez’s hospital “team manager,” who told Sibayan this.
“Residents are not allowed inside the room,” said Sibayan.
Asked whether it was unusual for a resident doctor to be barred from a room, Sibayan answered in the affirmative.

According to Sibayan, apart from Torres, two other physicians made separate diagnoses of Romualdez — cardiologist Rody Sy and neurologist Rogelio Libarres. He said he was only tasked with adding the diagnoses to the medical abstract.

On Thursday, the 3rd Division transferred Romualdez’s custody from the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) to the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology. After the resolution on his request for hospital confinement, the former speaker will be detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.
The court also scheduled Romualdez’s arraignment on September 7, the phase where he will be read his case and asked to enter either a guilty or not-guilty plea.
Echoing what Interior Secretary Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla had said, the doctors confirmed that Romualdez checked in at around 4 pm.
CIDG Metro Manila chief Police Colonel John Guiagui said the former speaker has moved to another hospital room, which is being guarded by law enforcers.

Torres said on Thursday that months ago, staff of Romualdez asked him if he would be willing to manage the former speaker’s hospital care. He accepted, so he formed a team of specialists to take care of Romualdez.

On September 7, the doctor said he received a call from Romualdez’s staff between 9 am and 10 am because the congressman complained of chest pains. Due to the former speaker’s history of heart problems, Torres immediately suggested confinement for Romualdez so he could be examined.

But why was Romualdez confined immediately, bypassing the emergency room? Torres explained that, in consultation with Sy, they advised the former speaker to be admitted for confinement and evaluation.
And if Romualdez had already complained of chest pains that morning, why did they wait until 4 pm to admit him?
“[Maybe] he wanted my advice,” said Torres.

blocks.caption: Apart from timing, what else is ‘unusual’ about Romualdez’s hospital confinement?

blocks.text: Romualdez is in a private room and not under intensive care. Torres said his patient needed “active monitoring.”
“It can be an impending heart attack, unstable angina,” said the physician.

Further, Torres said it was “high risk” to transport Romualdez because of the possibility of a heart attack. This was raised repeatedly because Remulla had earlier said the former speaker should be transferred to the PNP General Hospital in Camp Crame — and, of course, given the court’s commitment order for Romualdez, to Payatas.
The 3rd Division will continue the hearing on Friday, September 11, when more of Romualdez’s doctors are expected to take the witness stand. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Our forefathers are coming back’: Naga people celebrate after Oxford museum agrees to return remains
articles.summary:
Following six years of talks, Pitt Rivers Museum will return body parts collected by British colonial administrators to north-east India

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland,…

blocks.text: Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.

On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”

Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.

The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.

The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.

blocks.caption: Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist (kneeling, centre, in a red scarf) with other Naga delegates and museum staff.  Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”

In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.

“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”

The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.

The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.

blocks.caption: Members of the Naga delegation view the relics on display at the Pitt Rivers Museum. Photograph: Pitt Rivers Museum

blocks.text: “They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”

Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

articles.title: Police did not intervene as Canada's most prolific voyeur was 'looking for more victims,' court records show
articles.summary: Saanich police watched but did not intervene for over a month as Canada's most prolific voyeur strode through businesses with a phone in hand while out on bail, in breach of bail conditions. Court…

image.caption: A Value Village thrift store in downtown Victoria, B.C. A Crown lawyer claimed Yin Yeung Derek Chan was under police observation as when the voyeur hunted for victims in locations like Fitness World and Value Village, where Chan had previously recorded hundreds of women and girls. (Mike McArthur/CBC

blocks.text: British Columbia·CBC Investigates

Saanich police watched but did not intervene for over a month as Canada's most prolific voyeur strode through businesses with a phone in hand while out on bail, in breach of bail conditions. Court records obtained by CBC News reveal that a Crown lawyer believed Yin Yeung Derek Chan was on the hunt for more victims in Fitness World and Value Village, where the voyeur had previously recorded hundreds of women and girls.
Businesses in which voyeur broke bail conditions were never contacted by police, companies say
Saanich police watched but did not intervene for over a month as Canada's most prolific voyeur strode through businesses with a phone in hand in breach of bail conditions.

According to court records obtained by CBC News, a Crown lawyer claimed Yin Yeung Derek Chan was under police observation as the voyeur hunted for victims in locations like Fitness World and Value Village, where Chan had previously recorded hundreds of women and girls.

Chan, who filmed at least 652 women and girls in Greater Victoria in what officials claim is the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada, was later sentenced to four and a half years in jail after being convicted of voyeurism and child pornography charges.

CBC News has listened to courtroom submissions in the case, which cast light on the Saanich Police Department investigation. Those records, along with victim impact statements and interviews with victims, raise questions about why police did not act to stop the voyeur sooner.

Saanich police did not answer questions from CBC News for this story, but said in a statement that the department's decisions took a trauma-informed approach to avoid "actions that could contribute to further victimization."
Businesses Chan visited while violating bail conditions say they were never contacted by police.
"We are deeply concerned by the reported conduct and the impact it had on those affected," said Value Village in a statement.

Police found thousands of images and more than 100 hours of videos of women and children in Chan's home prior to the voyeur's arrest in April 2024. Chan was released on bail that month, with a condition not to use a cellphone outside of the home.
Despite that condition, Saanich police observed Chan using multiple cellphones in public on at least three occasions over a month before Chan was re-arrested on Jan. 30, 2025.
On Dec. 27, 2024, police observed Chan using a cellphone at Uptown shopping centre, entering a Fitness World gym, and using the phone inside the gym.
Police watched as Chan returned to the gym on Jan. 7, 2025, and used a phone in the gym again.

On Jan. 9, Chan used two cellphones in a Tim Hortons parking lot and was seen on a phone at Fitness World. Then, police followed Chan to Value Village in Victoria where the voyeur spent an hour and a half with a cellphone in hand.

The majority of Chan's victims prior to his initial arrest — more than 400 women and children — were secretly recorded while at Value Village, according to statements made in court by Crown lawyer Paul Cheeseman.
"That's exactly where his offending behaviour was, at these gyms and at Value Village, so the circumstances of the breach was that he was … out looking for more victims," Cheeseman told the judge.

For years prior to arrest, Chan found ways to thwart court orders aimed at preventing further voyeurism. The voyeur secretly recorded hundreds of women while on bail following an arrest for voyeurism in 2019.
Chan served 60 days in jail for that offence in 2022. During that same year, Chan filmed more than one video every other day, breaching probation and failing to complete court-ordered counselling.
Police have responsibility to prevent harm, former IIO head says

Ashley Dryburgh, executive director of the Victoria Sexual Assault Centre, which has been helping victims impacted by Chan's crimes, believes the police didn't do enough to alert and protect the community from the risks Chan posed.

"I am deeply disappointed to hear that the perpetrator was on bail [for months] and police seemingly had evidence of his continuation of committing crimes and violating his bail conditions, and it took a month to re-arrest the perpetrator," she said.
"Were people being used as bait to build a case to support this person?"

items: B.C. attorney general says potential victims of Saanich voyeur have 'right to know' key details from police

blocks.text: Saanich police did not respond to specific questions from CBC News for this story, including how many people Chan recorded while out on bail.

But Deputy Chief Const. Damian Kowalewich said in a statement that the department shared information with the public where it could, but based decisions on what to release on an intention to protect victims' privacy and avoid causing them further harm.

"Throughout the investigation, our priorities were to identify victims, support those affected, protect their privacy, hold the offender accountable, and take reasonable steps to reduce the risk of further victimization," wrote Kowalewich.

"We recognized from the outset that these were deeply personal and intrusive offences, and our approach was guided by a trauma-informed commitment to minimizing further harm while supporting victims through the criminal justice process."

Police have a responsibility to prevent harm if they believe the public is at risk, said Ron MacDonald, the former chief civilian director of B.C.'s Independent Investigations Office, which is a civilian-led police oversight agency. In this case, he says voyeurism poses a "serious psychological harm."

"One could certainly make an argument that he ought to have been arrested as soon as he was seen outside of the home with a cellphone, because that's a clear violation of his court order," said MacDonald, who added that without full details from police it is difficult to know why they did not take this action.
Outstanding questions remain
As Chan's crimes came to light publicly for the first time in the wake of the sentencing, community group chats and social media comments bubbled with anxiety.
Women and girls across southern Vancouver Island wondered the same thing: am I or is someone I know a victim?
One victim, whose identity is protected by a publication ban, told CBC News it's a concern.
"I feel like every single woman and girl in Victoria, like anywhere, could have been a victim at any time during those years, and like, how are you supposed to know?" she said.

items: 1st known victim of Saanich voyeur calls for police, court reforms to prevent future offences

blocks.text: About 40 victims were identified by police prior to the sentencing. Police will not say how many more victims they have confirmed since.
Officers uploaded images of women and girls to an AI model earlier this year to help find victims and additional videos created by Chan, according to a police report read at the sentencing hearing.
From this, one officer found a site where six videos, featuring known victims and one unknown victim, had garnered more than 100,000 views.
In the statement provided by Kowalewich, the deputy chief constable wrote that he understands Chan's crimes will continue to have effects long after the sentencing.
"We understand that some victims may still be seeking answers, information, or support as they continue to process the impact of these offences," he wrote.
"Our commitment to those affected remains ongoing, and support remains available for those who may require it."
With files by Jason Proctor

articles.title: Business owners say Regina's tent encampment is hurting neighbourhood
articles.summary: The encampment in Pepsi Park has been steadily growing this summer, now reaching 70 tents and some 150 people. The city has moved to an outreach approach, rather than dismantling it. While some…

image.caption: A tent encampment in Regina's Pepsi Park has been growing steadily over the course of the summer. That's a cause for concern for Ron Fellinger of Fellinger & Son's Meats who says it's hurting his business. (Colleen Silverthorn/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan

The encampment in Pepsi Park has been steadily growing this summer, now reaching 70 tents and some 150 people. The city has moved to an outreach approach, rather than dismantling it. While some advocates call for more supports like showers and electricity, business owners say it's costing them.
This owner says encampment should be dismantled, as advocates call for more supports in Pepsi Park
When Ron Fellinger steps outside of his business, Fellinger & Son's Meats, he can't help but think of how Regina's Heritage neighbourhood has changed in the last 50-some years.
"This park used to be a park for children to come and play. They played soccer, they played baseball," he said, adding he's worked in the area since the 1960s.
"You don't see anyone anymore … this is supposed to be a public park."
An encampment in Pepsi Park has steadily grown through the summer, from a few tents earlier in the year to an estimated 150 people sleeping in about 70 tents now.

The neighbourhood has been home to previous tent encampments, which have been torn down by the city in the past. But the City of Regina has pivoted to what it describes as a more person-centred approach, focusing on providing outreach support to help people get better shelter.
Businesses in Regina’s Heritage neighbourhood raise concerns about encampment

Businesses were recently invited to a meeting with city representatives to share their concerns, but Fellinger said he didn't attend, not having faith that his views would be heard. He said customers are turned off from coming into the store, seeing some of the societal dysfunction unfolding outside.
He disagrees with the city's approach in allowing the encampment to stay up.
"They're enabling these people, and there are going to be more and more people like [this] coming to the neighbourhoods in Regina," he said, adding tents don't belong in residential areas.
Jarrid Linder, service manager at Downtown Automatic Transmission, said his business has also seen more break-ins as the encampment grew.
"In the past probably two or three months, we've changed 17 windows on customers' vehicles from break-ins," he said.
"It's kind of a free-for-all out there."
Advocates say support is what's needed
The city has provided portable toilets at the site, but advocates and volunteers are saying people in the camp need showers, storage and power.
"To be clear, the services here are a very incredibly low-bar right now. We need a lot of help," said advocate and volunteer Shawn Koch.
He added that no one chooses to be without a home, but treating people with dignity goes a long way to improving their circumstances.

"When we've written off an entire group of people and dehumanize them in such a way, all it really takes is just a little bit of human contact and mutual respect, and you can see people growing and getting better," Koch said.
There's been a benefit to having people gathered in one spot, being able to implement rules against stealing each other's property and checking that no one overdoses, he said.

Showers and toilets are ways to protect people's dignity, Koch added, comparing this to Saskatoon's approach, which has been to dismantle encampments over concerns about safety risks for users and the risk of catastrophic fires.
LISTEN | These politicians describe how their cities are dealing with encampments:
Blue Sky51:23Cities grapple with ways to deal with tent encampments
Regina city councillor Victoria Flores, who represents the area, spearheaded Tuesday's meeting with business representatives, inviting people to share what they've been seeing and hearing.
The Heritage neighbourhood has long grappled with issues of housing insecurity and poverty, she acknowledged.
"But, of course, there's a heightened feeling of maybe safety-related issues," she said.
Flores said she was heartened to hear people expressing concerns not just for themselves, their businesses and customers, but also for the people living in encampments.

"I think what is clear is nobody wants to live in an encampment and no one wants to have an encampment around it, right?" she said. "What we need to do is find solutions that provide dignity and safety for everybody involved."
Homeless encampment deters customers, Regina business says
Both Koch and Flores said other levels of government need to step in to make housing more readily available, while also providing addictions treatment and mental health supports.
"The solution there is finding housing with wraparound supports that meet people where they're at," Flores said.
Permanent housing is the dream for encampment residents like Nevada Adams.
The 31-year-old has been on the streets for a year, trying to stay warm and dry in all kinds of weather, from –50 C in winter to the hard rain of last weekend.
Over the past few weeks, Adams said he's been working to get identification so he can be put on a housing list. In the meantime, he's been doing his bit to keep the camp clean of garbage and debris.
"The people that don't have it rough like this, [they] tend to look down on us. But they don't see what they go through, they don't see the battles we go through," Adams said.
"They have no idea what it's like."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Janani Whitfield is a community engagement producer who also edits feature storytelling and First Person columns for CBC Saskatchewan. Contact her at janani.whitfield@cbc.ca.
with files from CBC's Nichole Huck, Colleen Silverthorn, Blue Sky and The Morning Edition

articles.title: Europe needs to compete in spaceflight, says France's Macron
articles.summary: The French president called for setting goals like European cargo missions, lunar landings, and crewed spaceflight while urging the bloc to reduce its reliance on US and Russia.

image.caption: A French 'Ariane-6' rocket takes off from Europe's spaceport in French GuianaImage: Ronan Lietar/AFP

blocks.text: French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called on Europe to strengthen its space sector to close the gap with the United States and China.
"Space Europe is still weak," he said during a discussion at the International Space Summit in Paris.
European-crewed spaceflight
"We want Europe to assert its ambition in crewed spaceflight," he said. "Our European space program remains fragile and we must step up our efforts."
Macron said in two years, he wants to see the "first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station."
He added that in five years, he would like to see the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, "land on the Moon's surface."
"And in 10 years' time, I want to see the first European crewed capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board."
Kourou, located in French Guiana, is home to the European Union's primary spaceport.

The French president also said Europe needs to reduce its dependence on US and Russian services. At the moment, Europe's space exploration relies on rockets and satellites from the United States and Russia for communication and surveillance.
ESA's PLATO mission — the search for another Earth
'Passengers or pilots?'
Although the the European Space Agency(ESA) secured a record budget of over €22 billion in 2025 to cover programs for three years, it has never sent a crewed mission into space.
After Macron's speech, Josef Aschbacher, director general of the European Space Agency (ESA), remarked: "Are we passengers or pilots?"
The ESA head emphasized that countries around the world are rapidly developing space technology from the "critical infrastructure" of satellites to lunar exploration.
"In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities," he said.
Aschbacher added that if Europe wants to achieve independence in space exploration, it must invest around €1 billion annually ($1.1 billion).
"Dependency comes at a cost. The gap with world leaders in the space sector is widening, both financially and technologically."
Europe's new space milestone

articles.title: The dynasties, elites, and parties competing for power in BARMM
articles.summary: Thirteen regional political parties and nearly 700 candidates from dynasties and those with ties to the MILF and MNLF are vying for power in the Bangsomoro Parliament

blocks.text: Decades of conflict and peacebuilding will culminate on Monday, September 14 — the day when more than two million Filipinos of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will cast their votes in the regional parliamentary elections.

The momentous elections matter not just because it is the first of its kind but because the Bangsamoro people will decide the set of leaders that will hopefully overcome the region’s challenges of self-governance and its history of neglect and underdevelopment.

The people’s memory of the Moro struggle, infused with the trauma of rido (clan feuds), poverty, and the threat of insurgency, will be tested as the list of candidates contains aspirants belonging to the region’s powerful political dynasties and former combatants, whose loyalties lie with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the Moro National Liberation Front or MNLF.

We’ve compiled the profiles of the candidates running in the region’s 32 districts and the 13 regional political parties all eyeing a seat in the Bangsamoro Parliament. More than just looking at family connections, the articles below also reviewed the historical rivalries and recent connections formed prior to election day.
Here are the dynasties, elites, and parties vying for power in BARMM.
There are 13 regional political parties and nearly 700 candidates seeking seats in the Bangsamoro Parliament.

While this political participation in the region may broaden and offer BARMM voters a wider range of choices, the Asian Network for Free Elections and other watchdog groups say that the heightened tensions between the parties — made worse by clan and dynastic politics — could raise concerns over peace and security during the election period.
Watch this video by Shay Du for a rundown of the political parties participating in the historic polls.

blocks.caption: The dynasties, elites, and parties competing for power in BARMM

blocks.text: Over two dozen members of political dynasties, Islamic scholars, lawmakers, and youth leaders are competing for Lanao del Sur’s seats in the Bangsamoro region

The candidates have until September 12 to campaign in their respective districts. The province has 1,164 barangays and 727,634 registered voters, according to Commission on Elections data as of May 8.
Here are the electoral races in Lanao del Sur’s nine districts.

BARMM Interim Chief Minister Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua is running in the 3rd parliamentary district of Maguindanao del Norte, where the election results could determine whether he stays or not as the region’s leader.

If Macacua wins in the September elections, he would be eligible and could be chosen by the BARMM Parliament as the first elected chief minister of the seven-year-old region. This makes the election outcome in the Maguindanao del Norte district crucial, as it could determine the direction of the region.
Here are the electoral races happening in Maguindanao del Norte’s five parliamentary districts.
Relatives of the Midtimbang, Ampatuan, Upam, and Mangudadatu clans are vying for power in Maguindanao del Sur’s five parliamentary districts.

Maguindanao del Sur is currently led by Governor Ali Musa Midtimbang, whose family formed an alliance with the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) during the 2025 local election. Ali’s nephew, Member of Parliament Tawakal Midtimbang, is running in the 1st District.

The elder Midtimbang’s seat was previously held by Mariam Sangki Mangudadatu, the last governor of the once-undivided Maguindanao, whose relative is now vying for a seat in the Bangsamoro Parliament through Maguindanao del Sur’s 4th District.
Here are the electoral races happening in Maguindanao del Sur.

The Hatamans are seeking a larger foothold in Basilan’s delegation to the BARMM Parliament, with former Basilan governor and now Vice Governor Hadjiman “Jim” Hataman-Salliman’s son, Jimael Salam Datumanong Salliman, and nephew, Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) Member Abrar Hataman, seeking seats in the 4th and 3rd districts, respectively.
If they win, the Hatamans would hold two of Basilan’s four parliamentary seats. Both are running under the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), now led by Macacua.
Here are the electoral races happening in the province of Basilan.

blocks.caption: People, Person, Head

blocks.text: In Tawi-Tawi’s four parliamentary districts, members of political clans, former local officials, civil society leaders, and professionals are campaigning for seats in the 80-member Bangsamoro Parliament. More than half of them have ties to local political families.

One of three Que brothers from Bongao is seeking the 1st District’s parliamentary seat. The Matba, Amilbangsa, Matolo, Jamalul, and Ahaja clans also have members in the races for the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th districts. Tawi-Tawi Governor Yshmael Sali’s sister-in-law, Rhosatina Sulayman Matolo-De Asis, is among those seeking a seat in the 3rd District.
Here are the electoral races in Tawi-Tawi’s four districts.

Cotabato City, the seat of the Bangsamoro regional government, is seeing a competitive race among seasoned public officials, educators, and other candidates, some of whom have ties to local political dynasties.

Three parliamentary seats are up for grabs in the city, whose local government until recently was led by a mayor, Mohammad Ali “Bruce” Matabalao, who supported the UBJP, the political party of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
However, internal rifts in the MILF and the resignation of Matabalao from the UBJP have brought much speculation as to how well the MILF’s party is going to fare in Cotabato City’s 37 barangays.
Here are the electoral races in the three parliamentary districts of Cotabato City.

articles.title: MARINA investigates Coron ship fire
articles.summary: The Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) is already looking into the fire incident on a vessel in Coron, Palawan that killed five individuals.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 6:42pm
The Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) is already looking into the fire incident on a vessel in Coron, Palawan that killed five individuals.
MARINA said that an investigation team was already deployed and assured assistance to the 43 survivors.

"The Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) has immediately deployed an investigation team and mobilized teams from the MARINA Regional Office IV to actively coordinate with the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and provide assistance to the survivors following the fire incident involving passenger vessel MV 'June Aster' in the vicinity of Barangay Marcilla, Coron, Palawan, on 9 September 2026," the agency said.
"MARINA’s Enforcement Service (ES) has also commenced a Marine Safety Investigation to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident," it added.
MARINA added that it will help continue to provide updates once verified information is available.
According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the fire on MV June Aster started in the cargo hold based on the initial account of one of the survivors.
The surviving crew member told authorities that the fire started small.

But authorities have yet to obtain the complete details of how the fire started, as the surviving crew member interviewed by the PCG has yet to provide a full account of the incident. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Vance appears to walk back Trump’s offer of $5,000 ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms – US politics live
articles.summary: Vice-president suggests payment would not go to all and would be paid for by tariff revenues despite supreme court rulings against much of Trump’s program

blocks.text: Vance appears to walk back Trump claims that US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Vice-president JD Vance appeared to partially row back on Donald Trump’s outlandish claims that every adult citizen in the US would receive $5,000 if the Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour long speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”.

But Vance, speaking after the president, suggested the so-called dividend payments would not go to the wealthy and that it could be paid for by US tariff revenues – though the suggested payment dwarfs what the US has taken in through the protectionist measures.

Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed US tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president’s tariff program last year.
The White House has yet to release details on Trump’s announcement.

Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.”

The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely.
Read the full story here:
In other developments:

items: In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by pleading with Republicans to “pretend that I’m running”. The president centered himself in the battle to control Congress, and acknowledged that candidates are more successful when he is on the ballot. He offered an ominous outlook if Republicans fail to retain power.

Throughout his remarks, Trump also tried to campaign on behalf of Republicans in competitive midterm races. While he made fun of Ken Paxton’s clothing choices and the way he speaks, he praised the Republican nominee for US Senate in Texas as “the single greatest attorney general” in the state’s history, while also branding his opponent James Talarico as a “disaster”.

Earlier, Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing.

Meanwhile, several Republicans who are facing tough races have chosen not to attend the convention in Dallas. This include Susan Collins, the five-term incumbent senator from Maine, and Dan Sullivan – the Republican senator from Alaska who is facing a tough contest against former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 19m agoVance appears to walk back Trump claims that US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms

blocks.text: Marc Goldwein, the senior policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a think tank in Washington, said Donald Trump has no authority send money to Americans without approval from Congress.
Goldwein added that dividends are something that companies pay when there’s a surplus, but the US is running $2tn annual deficits and has $40tn in debt.
“The idea that we’ve had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable,” he said. “We don’t have surpluses to give away.”

The move was reminiscent of billionaire Elon Musk’s efforts to buy votes in last year’s Wisconsin state Supreme Court race, where he handed out million-dollar checks to voters to try to boost a candidate who ultimately lost.
Trump’s proposal would be legal because the payment would go to everyone regardless of how they voted, or whether they voted at all, said New Mexico-based attorney John Day.
“This is a campaign promise,” Day said. “It’s not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way.”

articles.title: Marcos wants Zaldy Co arrested 'at all costs;' DILG sets two week-timeline
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. wants dismissed House lawmaker Zaldy Co arrested “at all costs,” Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Thursday.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 6:38pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. wants dismissed House lawmaker Zaldy Co arrested “at all costs,” Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Thursday.

Co, tagged as a mastermind behind the multi-billion flood control scam, has been evading Philippine authorities since 2025. Remulla is set to fly to France with the intention of bringing back the fugitive ex-lawmaker.

“That’s the agenda, that’s the agenda. Zaldy Co is the agenda … we know where he is, we know the address, we know his house. It’s to get him back here,” Remulla said in an ambush interview after the Department of the Interior and Local Government’s budget hearing at the Senate.
Remulla said that he was confident that Co could be brought back home, saying that Marcos wanted to get Co back “at all costs.”
“The truth and the law are behind us and I think we can conclusively prove that once the warrant of arrest is in order,” he said.
Asked for a target, Remulla estimated that it could take “two weeks.”
Remulla is hoping that a Red Notice will be issued by the Interpol. It is another reason why he is going to France.
Despite the lack of a Red Notice, however, Remulla said that it would still be difficult for Co to move around Europe.
Co has not sent out feelers to the government, Remulla said.

“I don't know the man. I've never met him. If I did, I don't recall, I've never had his number, we've never had contact with each other. We’ll only get in touch with him when we arrest him,” Remulla said.
Asked where his confidence is coming from, Remulla said “mayabang ako”. (I am boastful.) — RSJ GMA News

articles.title: ICC prosecution: Verify open-source materials on a case-by-case basis
articles.summary: After the defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to require expert verification for open-source materials, the prosecution urged Trial Chamber…

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 6:24pm

After the defense team of former President Rodrigo Duterte asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to require expert verification for open-source materials, the prosecution urged Trial Chamber III to reject the request, saying the need for such verification should be determined on a case-by-case basis.
In a document dated September 9 and posted on the ICC website, ad interim Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang opposed the defense’s request to amend the E-Court Protocol.

“Open-source and user-generated evidence are extremely broad categories of documents that capture numerous types of evidence. As such, whether open-source or user-generated evidence requires an accompanying expert report should be determined on case-by-case basis by the submitting party that has the burden of establishing its relevance, probative value and assessing its potential prejudicial effect,” Niang said.
“It is unreasonable, unnecessary and against the interests of judicial efficiency, to require an expert report to accompany all forms of open-source and user-generated evidence,” he added.
On September 4, Duterte’s defense team asked the ICC chamber to amend the E-Court Protocol regarding open-source materials.
Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes argued that the prosecution’s evidence had ballooned since the charges were confirmed, increasing from around 5,000 items to 25,000.

Haynes said the evidence reviewed by the defense so far was of “poor quality,” alleging that some were duplicates. He also said that, amid rampant “fake news” surrounding the case, merely providing a URL was not enough to verify the authenticity of an item of evidence.
“The Defense is deeply concerned that the quality and quantity of the evidence in this case risks flooding the record with unreliable and/or irrelevant material,” Haynes said.

“It is proposed that such expert verification reports, which can cover multiple items of evidence, should always accompany open source and user-generated evidence submitted to the Chamber in the present case,” he added.

Niang, however, said the defense’s proposed amendment would require an expert report for all forms of open-source materials. Given the broad range of materials that may fall under the category, he said the need for expert verification should instead be assessed separately for each item.

For example, publicly available reports from organizations such as the United Nations and Human Rights Watch, as well as reputable news publications, should not automatically require expert evidence, Niang said.
“Chambers of this Court have consistently allowed the submission of open-source evidence of this nature without the need for an accompanying expert report,” Niang said.

The prosecution acknowledged that the court must remain vigilant in assessing open-source material amid the rise of artificial intelligence and online disinformation, but said the response should be proportionate to the risks. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Quiboloy lodges libel complaints vs. Hontiveros, House lawmakers
articles.summary: Pastor Apollo Quiboloy has lodged libel complaints against Senator Risa Hontiveros, Akbayan Partylist Representative Perci Cendaña, and ML Partylist Representative Leila de Lima.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 6:20pm

Detained pastor Apollo Quiboloy has lodged libel complaints against Senator Risa Hontiveros and House lawmakers Akbayan Partylist Representative Perci Cendaña and ML Partylist Representative Leila de Lima.
The lawmakers confirmed the complaints in separate statements.

Hontiveros, who oversaw the Senate hearings that brought forward Quiboloy’s alleged victims, said that she was not afraid of anything, adding that Quiboloy should face the cases filed against him instead of trying to turn the discussion on its head.
Quiboloy is accused of heavy crimes such as human trafficking, sexual abuse and child abuse, said Hontiveros.

“Ang dapat nating protektahan ay ang mga biktima at kababayan nating naglakas-loob magsalita at lumantad laban kay Quiboloy. Hangga’t humihingi sila ng hustisya, tatayo ako sa tabi nila,” Hontiveros said in a statement on Thursday.
(The ones we should protect are the victims and our countrymen that were brave and came forward against Quiboloy. As long as they seek justice, I stand next to them.)
Meanwhile, De Lima said that the cyber libel case is misdirecting the issue. Quiboloy must answer for his crimes, she added.

“Let us not waste government resources for this baseless case. Huwag na silang magkunwari na biktima siya ng cyber libel. Apollo Quiboloy is not a victim. Ipagtanggol na lang niya ang kanyang sarili sa kanyang mga kaso sa mga karumaldumal na krimen na panggagahasa at pagturing sa mga kababaihan bilang mga personal na kagamitan,” De Lima said.

(Let us not waste government resources for this baseless case. They should not act like victims of cyber libel. Apollo Quiboloy is not a victim. He should defend himself from his grievous crimes such as rape and treating women like personal objects.)
Cendaña said that it was an “honor” to be named alongside Hontiveros and De Lima in Quiboloy’s suit.

“Hindi kami titigil na ipaglaban ang katarungan para sa mga biktima ng kahayupan ni Quiboloy,” Cendaña said in a Facebook post. (We will not stop fighting for justice for the victims of Quiboloy’s depravity.)
In a statement on Thursday, the Akbayan Partylist called the charges “laughable.”

“Quiboloy enjoys being called all sorts of ridiculous things, but not things grounded in facts. Akbayan stands by the victims’ testimonies and the legal records in the Philippines and the United States,” the partylist said.
Quiboloy is currently detained at the Pasig City Jail Male Dormitory facing charges of qualified human trafficking and sexual abuse.

He is also wanted by the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation for sex trafficking charges and fraud, with Washington already filing an extradition request to gain custody of the televangelist.
GMA News has reached out to Quiboloy’s counsel for a statement. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Bayeux Tapestry goes on display at sold-out London exhibit
articles.summary: The nearly 1,000 year-old, 70-meter-long tapestry is considered a symbol of UK-France friendship. More than 100,000 tickets have been sold.

image.caption: The Bayeux Tapestry will be on display in London until next JulyImage: Suzanne Plunkett/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London opened Thursday to much fanfare, in what British newspaper the Times has dubbed "Tapestry-mania," with more than 100,000 tickets already sold.

The tapestry is on loan from France, and comes after years of diplomacy, with the move being seen as a symbol of close ties between Paris and London. It is thought to be the first time the tapestry has gone on display outside of France.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the tapestry's loan a "return," while King Charles III hailed the move as a "precious symbol of trust at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."
The work is believed to have been made in England nearly 1,000 years ago before finding its way to Bayeux, now located in the French region of Normandy.

Two previous attempts to loan the Bayeux Tapestry to the UK were unsuccessful. Once was in 1953 for the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, and again in 1966 for the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings, which is depicted on the tapestry.

blocks.caption: King Charles III, Queen Camilla alongside France's President Emmanuel Macron at a preview event in LondonImage: Adrian Dennis/AFP

blocks.text: What is the Bayeux Tapestry?
The Bayeux Tapestry is a 70-meter long artwork, which is thought to be incomplete, depicting the Norman conquest of England in 1066.

Norman forces led by William the Conqueror were able to defeat and dethrone King Harold Godwinson in a campaign culminating in victory at the Battle of Hastings. The tapestry famously depicts Harold being shot in the eye with an arrow, as he is said to have died — admittedly in what modern historians believe is likely a myth or artistic exaggeration.

This conquest was a crucial contributing moment in the establishment of what would become England and later the British Empire and the UK. It was the last of several successful foreign invasions of England in a millennium, and turned out to be the last one for a millennium

blocks.caption: The Bayeux Tapestry is thought to be nearly 1,000 years old Image: Pascal Deloche/Godong/picture alliance

blocks.text: The conquest also added the final core ingredient, French, to the linguistic melting pot that produced the modern English language.

The embroidered cloth, which has brief Latin titles captioning its 58 scenes, is widely accepted to have been made in England as a tribute to William after his victory. It was then transported to his family home in Normandy.
The Bayeux Tapestry will be on display at London's British Museum until next July.

articles.title: Nearly 2 in 3 Pinoys back COA order for VP Sara to return P73 million — poll
articles.summary: The survey found that most Filipinos want the disallowed P73 million confidential funds to be returned.

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 6:08pm
Members of the prosecution team present boxes labeled “Confidential Funds” during the 11th day of the Senate impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte in Pasay City on Aug. 3, 2026.
Senate of the Philippines via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — A recent survey found that nearly two in every three Filipinos want Vice President Sara Duterte to return the P73.28 million in disallowed confidential funds to the government.

Based on the latest results of The National Momentum Survey by Momentum Research, 64% of Filipinos say they agree or strongly agree with the Commission on Audit (COA) order that obliged Duterte to return the allegedly misused funds.
In 2024, COA issued a notice of disallowance on part of the 2022 OVP confidential funds after it found that the funds were spent on activities that are unrelated to their declared purposes.
Only 24% said they disagree or strongly disagree, 8.9% said they are unsure, and 3.1% refused to answer.
Younger gen want the funds back
The survey found that, in terms of age, most of those who believed that Duterte should comply with the COA order came from the younger generation.
“Almost 4 in 5 Gen Zs believe the vice president should comply with the COA order, while 3 in 5 Millennials share the same view,” the survey read.
Most of the respondents from Generation X, or 56.1%, also believed that the allegedly misused confidential funds should be returned to the state.

Meanwhile, it was also observed that 52.7% of respondents belonging to the Baby Boomers and the Silent Generation backed the COA order, which “do not show a clear majority in support considering the margin of error” according to the survey.

The National Momentum Survey was carried out through face-to-face interviews with 1,487 adults across the country from August 18 to 23, with a ±2.5 percentage-point national margin of error at a 95% confidence level.

articles.title: 97-year-old Guelph, Ont., man skydives in quest to 'learn as much as I can about life'
articles.summary: James Gordon, a resident of the Village of Riverside Glen retirement community in Guelph, Ont., jumped from a plane at an altitude of about 4,200 metres last month in his first skydiving adventure.…

image.caption: 'I feel that if you push yourself and you do things, you keep your mind working and you keep your body working, the more chance you have that you will live longer,' Gordon says. (Skydive SWOOP)

blocks.text: Kitchener-Waterloo

James Gordon, a resident of the Village of Riverside Glen retirement community in Guelph, Ont., jumped from a plane at an altitude of about 4,200 metres last month in his first skydiving adventure. 'I spun over, round and round, all over the place,' the spunky senior says.
James Gordon says he may do it again when he turns 100
'An experience never to be forgotten': 97-year-old Guelph man goes skydiving
At 97, James Gordon of Guelph, Ont., is proving you’re never too old for a new adventure.
In his first time skydiving, the resident of the Village of Riverside Glen retirement community jumped from a plane at an altitude of 4,200 metres last month.
“I wanted to do it because it’s an unusual experience,” he said. “I just wanted the experience and to say I’ve done something else. I want to learn as much as I can about life.”
The retirement community partners with Skydive Swoop in Dundas so residents can try skydiving.
Gordon is the oldest resident to take on the challenge. He says the jump is part of his quest to live an “exciting and thrilling” life.
He said he was eager to get up in the air, but did begin having second thoughts the night before.
“I was really, really caught up with feeling very unsure if I wanted to continue. But my wife was there, so I behaved with a little bit of courage and just waited for the next morning.”
He said that when it came time to jump, he was no longer afraid.
“The next morning when I had to go get on the plane, my golly, I didn’t feel a thing. I was just interested."
Taking the plunge
On Aug. 21, Gordon piled into a plane with three others.
He was strapped to an experienced skydiver.
During the leap, Gordon said, he was immediately caught off guard.
“I never knew I’d be tumbling, turning and twisting. I spun over, round and round, all over the place.”
Once he stabilized, he was able to enjoy the view.
“I really loved it, looking around, seeing things at a far distance. There were mountains, the hills, the lakes — everything you could wish to see."
Kimberly McCarthy, manifest manager at Skydive Swoop, said skydiving when older isn't as rare as some people may think.
"There's no age limit on skydiving," McCarthy said. "There are quite a few people out there that are still skydiving regularly and they're in their 80s."
McCarthy believes Gordon is the oldest skydiver Swoop has ever had. She didn't get to see the jump itself, but she was there when he landed.

"We were really excited for him. We all came running up to him, and gave him handshakes and high-fives. It's getting me choked up just thinking about it. I'm kind of getting old there myself, and so it just kind of gave me the feeling that I still had a whole half of my life coming my way."
A life of adventure
Daring experiences have always been a part of Gordon's life.
For five years, he worked as a game warden in Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe.
His daughter, Gillian Bakar, said she remembers countless stories from her childhood.
"His dog was eaten by an alligator at some point. He ran from elephants and escaped from lions. He had serious adventure back when the wild was truly wild."
Gordon also made contact with a number of tribes and built relationships with members.
When it came time for Gordon to take to the sky instead of the jungle, Bakar said, there was no hesitation on her end.
"My first thought was at 97, if you want to have an adventure like that, absolutely run with it," she said.
"I just feel absolutely happy for him. He's managed to do something that he is so incredibly proud of."
As for what's next, Gordon hopes to publish a book recounting his adventures in the jungle.
The book has been over 50 years in the making.
"His lifelong wish has been to get that book published," Bakar said.
Always in search of the next thrill, Gordon said he plans to skydive again when he turns 100.
He believes his hunger for adventure is his secret to a long life.
"I feel that if you push yourself and you do things, you keep your mind working and you keep your body working, the more chance you have that you will live longer. And here I am at 97."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Diego Pizarro is reporter/editor at CBC Kitchener-Waterloo and an associate producer for CBC Television: The National. You can reach him at diego.pizarro@cbc.ca

articles.title: Royal family rift after popular TV news presenter chosen to succeed Ugandan king
articles.summary: King Oyo's family say he left a will naming his young son as heir to the Tooro kingdom.

blocks.text: "My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.

Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".
She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday.
"I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."
Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.
His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday, and preparations for the funeral are under way.
Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.
Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.
The existence of Oyo's son was first publicly revealed in the days after the king's death by President Museveni, who said he had been told about the young boy by the queen mother.
No other details have officially been disclosed, and he had not previously been presented as Oyo's heir.
The disagreement has exposed the complicated way in which succession works in Tooro.
Unlike Britain's monarchy, where the crown passes according to an established line of succession, Tooro's monarch is chosen from the Babiito, the royal dynastic clan.

At a press conference in ​the kingdom's capital of Fort Portal, the royal clan's succession committee announced Kijanangoma, Oyo's cousin and a news presenter ​at the state-run broadcaster UBC, as monarch.
The clan elders said they had the customary authority to choose a suitable prince to become "the Omukama" - the local title for the king of Tooro.
The succession panel said it had carried out "due diligence, consultation and adequate consideration" before selecting Kijanangoma, with 19 members signing the resolution.
Kijanangoma is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of former Tooro king George David Rukidi III.
Another royal, UK-based Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, was initially considered for the throne but declined, citing other responsibilities, according to the succession committee.
It is not yet clear when the enthronement will take place, but the committee said it would be conducted in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom.

articles.title: PH, South Korea partner for 1,500 new firetrucks - DILG
articles.summary: The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said on Thursday that it will deploy 1,500 firetrucks nationwide next year through an agreement with South Korea.

blocks.text: Published September 10, 2026 5:38pm
The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said on Thursday that it will deploy 1,500 firetrucks nationwide next year through an agreement with South Korea.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the firetrucks will be acquired through a government-to-government agreement with South Korea.
The DILG, the Office of the President, Department of Foreign Affairs, and Bureau of Fire Protection are coordinating with the South Korean government for the acquisition, he added.
“Within one and a half years, kumpleto na lahat ang munisipyo, wala na tayong magiging problema. Kumpleto na sa buong Pilipinas," said Remulla in a statement.
(Within one and a half years, every municipality will be fully equipped, and we won't have any more problems. It will be complete across the entire Philippines.)
“This is the cleanest transaction that is possible with the best possible benefit sa lahat ng mga Pilipino."
(This is the cleanest transaction possible, bringing the best possible benefit to all Filipinos.)
Meanwhile, the DILG turned over 20 Class 1 Unified 911 emergency response motorcycles to Police Regional Office 6 at Camp General Martin Teofilo B. Delgado in Iloilo City.
Of the 20 motorcycles, 10 were given to the Aklan Police Provincial Office and 10 others were turned over to the Iloilo City Police Office.
The DILG said the motorcycles will reinforce the emergency response following the rollout of the Unified 911.
The department said the system relies on geolocation to route callers to local emergency teams who can converse in the area's native language.
"Lahat ng mga language na ’yan, kung saan ka naroroon, kapag na-geotag ang tawag ninyo, ang sasagot sa inyo ay ang local language na," said Remulla.
(All of those languages—wherever you are located, once your call is geotagged, the person who answers will speak the local language.) —Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News

articles.title: 'People were trampling me': Philippine ferry fire survivor recalls narrow escape
articles.summary: A survivor has told the BBC of the chaos onboard as the ferry caught fire near the popular tourist spot of Coron.

blocks.text: Passengers on board a ferry to the Philippines' Palawan province were jolted into chaos on Wednesday night, when a fire broke out on the vessel.
Frantic cries pierced the night sky as hot air filled the boat, recalls Roland Lerma, one of more than 100 passengers aboard the MV June Aster.

Five people have died and 86 people are missing after the fire, which, in a country where shipping accidents are not uncommon, could become one of the deadliest maritime disasters the Philippines has seen.
Families are anxiously awaiting news about their loved ones on board, while survivors like Lerma are coming to terms with their harrowing escape.
Speaking to the BBC from a hospital in Coron, Lerma recalled that as the fire spread and he scrambled to get off the burning boat, he slipped and fell.
"When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," said the 30-year-old.
He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea.
He said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark.
"When I hit the water, I ditched all my possessions - the clothes I was wearing, phones, bags - so that I could float," he said.
Lerma said he floated on his back for about two hours before rescuers arrived and pulled him and other survivors out of the water.
"It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would have definitely died last night," he said.

Lerma, who works in construction, is from Leyte province. He had travelled to the capital Manila with five of his neighbours, where they boarded the ferry to bring them to work at Coron, a popular tourist spot in Palawan province.

According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the MV June Aster departed Manila's Port of Baseco on Tuesday night at 20:13 local time (12:13 GMT) and was scheduled to arrive at the Coron port at 18:00 on Wednesday.
But the ferry caught fire just 1.2 nautical miles (2.2km) off the coast of Coron's Marcilla village.
The fire was first reported at 18:45 local time on Wednesday night by a staff member of Atienza Shipping Lines, which owns the boat, the Coast Guard said.
The company said in a statement on Thursday that it was co-operating fully with authorities and expressed "profound sadness" about the fire.
Authorities say a survivor had told them the flames had started in the cargo hold after a loud explosion.
The ship had been carrying several motorcycles, an electric car, a forklift, a pick-up van and other goods, the Philippine Coast Guard said.
As the journey was expected to take more than 20 hours, passengers had slept on bunk beds onboard overnight.
Lerma said that two Chileans - a couple who looked like they were in their late 20s or early 30s - had slept in the beds next to his.
Authorities have since confirmed that two Chilean nationals were among the 43 people rescued.

Lerma and two of his neighbours are now in a hospital in Coron. Another person in their group has been taken to a bigger hospital in the neighbouring island of Culion, while two others remain missing, Lerma says.
"I have a couple of bruises and my chest is still hurting," Lerma said. "Last night, I had a hard time breathing. But I am okay now."
Search and rescue operations are ongoing, though authorities say the fire on the MV June Aster has still not been put out and there was visible smoke from the ferry.
A spokesperson for the Philippine Coast Guard said in a local television interview many of the survivors "are still in shock".
Meanwhile, families of the ferry's missing passengers are enduring an agonising wait.
Anelyn Magbanua told the BBC that her husband Marlon was on the ferry. He was returning to Coron after visiting Manila to see two of their children who are studying at the capital.
"He spent a couple of days there. He even sent me their pictures," she said.
She last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron.
Magbanua and her two-year-old son had gone to bed early on Wednesday night expecting Marlon to be home soon.
But she was woken up later that night by a relative who informed her that her husband's ferry had caught fire.
On Thursday she rushed to the hospital when she heard there was a chance her husband might be one of the rescued survivors there.
But officials have since told her that Marlon remains unaccounted for.
"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she told the BBC over the phone.
"I can't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night."
